what_it_does: Oblivious RAM (ORAM) is a technique that hides which memory addresses a program is accessing — useful when running code on an untrusted server where an observer tracking memory-access patterns could infer sensitive information. The price is steep: standard ORAM protocols impose large slowdowns because every memory operation triggers a whole sequence of additional memory operations that must finish one after another before the next can start, leaving the memory bus largely idle. Palermo redesigns a particular ORAM scheme called RingORAM so that multiple memory operations can overlap — both within a single logical ORAM request and across several requests happening simultaneously — without breaking the security guarantee that an attacker learns nothing from watching the access pattern. A dedicated hardware controller keeps track of which operations are genuinely dependent on each other (and thus must be ordered) versus which can safely run in parallel, and manages the internal data structures (a 'stash', a temporary holding area for data in transit, and a 'position map', a table that tracks where each data block is hidden in the ORAM tree) entirely in hardware to prevent overflow and to keep the pipeline moving.
